2560.body:
Margins are deposits meant to protect clearing members from possible default by other clearing members. There are two types of margin obligations: initial margin and variation margin. Whilst there are similarities in the ways initial and variation margins are calculated, different exchanges and Clearing Houses have their own proprietary methodologies.

The Initial Margin is a good faith deposit posted by the hedger with the financial counterparty of the hedge. The amount of Initial Margin is generally a small fraction of the contract value normally determined by the Clearing House or the financial institution selling the hedge. Initial Margin will occasionally be adjusted up or down to reflect increases or decreases in the commodity’s price volatility.

When the hedger liquidates a position, initial margin requirements are eliminated even though final disposition of the hedge profits and losses will not occur until the contracts settle on the settlement date.

Maintenance Margin

The Maintenance Margin represents the minimum amount of margin that must be maintained in an account. It is sometimes referred as a percentage of the Initial Margin.

Variation Margin

The Variation Margin is a variable margin payment that is made by clearing members to their respective Clearing Houses based upon adverse price movements of the futures contracts that these members hold. Every market day, financial institutions mark-to-market their customers’ outstanding futures positions using official market prices (normally published by the exchange and/or its Clearing House after the end of each trading day).

The mark-to-market process consists in comparing each original trade price of all contracts to the official market price for that maturity date. The difference is then multiplied by the volume of outstanding open paper position held. The result of this calculation gives a latent profit & loss (PnL) for the maturity date. The PnLs of all maturity dates are then added together to establish the total Variation Margin requirement.

Most commodity exchanges will require that customers having marked-to-market losses pay cash, via the Clearing House, to those customers showing marked-to-market profits. Inability by the hedger to face payment of margin calls and unless agreed with its financial counterparty gives the right to liquidate part or all of the outstanding paper positions at whatever price is available in the market. As a result, the hedger would be confronted to actual rather than latent losses and severe disruption to its hedging programme.

Margins and Credit Lines

Brokers who give access to exchanges may extend a Credit Line to their clients in order to cover Initial, Variation Margins or both. In practice, a Margin Call will be triggered when the relationship:

Credit Line + Maintenance Margin + Variation Margin + Collateral > 0

does not hold. If there is no Credit Line, the posted collateral (cash or securities) must cover for the margins.

In addtiion to organised market trades, there are bilateral trades.
2560.title: Margining

An option is a right but not an obligation to buy or sell an underlying contract at a predetermined price at a predefined date in the future. An option which conveys the right to buy called a Call; an option which conveys the right to sell is called a Put. Usually, options for commodities are Options on Futures rather than Options on Spot prices.

A Call option gives its buyer the right to buy a particular asset for an agreed price at a specified time in the future. A Put option gives its buyer the right to sell a particular asset for an agreed price at a specified time in the future.

The asset in this case will be a Commodity Futures. As Options for commodities are Options on Futures, Commodity Options will have the same parameters and features as Futures, namely:

In addition, Options have a

The Strike price or Exercise price of an option refers to the price level at which the contract can be exercised. The difference between the current Spot price and the Strike price (S-K) represents the gross profit of the trade.

An option can be described as “in-the-money” (ITM) if it would result in a profit if exercised immediately (i.e., the underlying forward price is above (below) the strike price for a call (put) option). An option which would result in loss of premium is “out of the money” (OTM) while it is “at the money” (ATM) if the underlying forward price is equal to the strike price. The profitability of an in-the- money purchased call option is similar to the profit potential of holding a long position in the underlying instrument. Out-of-the-money puts or calls offer potential profits, if they move as anticipated past at-the-money value into an in-the-money position.

Most Commodity Options on Futures are European or Asian.

Options can have cash settlements or settle into other contracts. It is quite common for European Options on Futures traded on Exchanges to settle into Futures positions:

Settlement dates for options contracts, therefore, need to be before settlement dates for Futures contracts.

3100.body:
A swap contract is in essence nothing more complex than a product that comprises a series of Futures contracts for different maturities intertwined. Futures are standardised contracts traded in an exchange while Swaps can be traded on Exchanges or trade as bilateral contracts between counterparties (OTC markets). Swaps bring flexibility at the time to hedge as and are most traded derivative product. The most common Swaps are the ones that use the monthly average price of a commodity as settlement price, which is usually in line with the physical markets. Quarterly pricing is also common.

As its name indicates, a Swap contract obliges two parties, to exchange or swap some specified cash flows at specified intervals of time (a month for example). At every specified maturity the buyer of the swap must pay a fixed amount of money (the price of the Swap) and the seller of the swap must pay a variable price (usually the average of the spot price over the specified interval). The difference between both prices is financially settled and exchange of commodity material does not exist.

This chapter requires some concepts developed in previous chapters, in particular Futures and Term Structure.

As is the case for Futures and Swaps, trading Options contracts implies a series of cash flows that result from margin requirements, premiums paid or received, commissions and settlement. These cash flows are exchanged between the hedger and the financial institution that provided the hedge.

Only Option writers need to be margined as buyers usually pay the Premium upfront. The values of the cash flows for initial and variation margins for Options are calculated using the following formulas:

Initial Margin for Options = Initial Premium * Quantity

Variation Margin for Options = MtM * Quantity

Initial margins are deposited at the inception of each trade while variation margins are posted when the daily mark to market requires it. In many cases, and particularly in OTC markets, hedge providers grant a Credit line to the hedgers and variations margins will not be called until such line is depleted.

Contrary to Futures and Swaps, where the initial exchange is done at zero cost, Options involve an initial cash flow that will depend on the market value for the Option (Premium).

Cash Flow from Premium = Premium * Quantity

In the case of a Options with Cash Settlement, only the differences between the daily prices and the contract price are financially settled.

Cash Flow from PnL = Option payoff

If the Option settles into a Futures contract, cash flows will be calculated accordingly.

Options: mark to market

During the life of the option, MtM is a measure of the fair market value of an Options position.

Mark to Market for Futures = Present Value (Current Value of the Option - Premium)

MtM = (VOt – Premium) * exp (-r*T)

Hedgers entering into Options contracts usually pay a commission charge that is negotiated with the Broker or established by the Exchange or Clearing House. The bid-offer spread and the shape of the curve can be seen as indirect costs but they are not recognised in any cash flow.

4000.body:
The performance of both financial and physical activities needs to be continuously monitored given the particularly volatile nature of commodity markets. In order to do so, a business reports the results of its business activity during determined periods of time. These reports are also a legal requirement for any operating business.

These accounts are critical as they measure the funds (in cash and credits) that the company needs to support the daily physical and financial operations.

A Cash account measures the immediately available funds. Cash is used to purchase physical material, pay operating and financial costs, pay financial settlements when unfavourable. In ordinary transactions, Cash is received from selling physical material and from favourable financial settlements.

A Credit line to trade derivatives establishes a maximum loan balance granted by financial institutions (bank or broker) to cover initial and variation margin requirements. The hedger can draw down on the line of credit at any time, as long as does not exceed the maximum set.

Financial Statements measure a business financial performance over a specific accounting period. The main Financial Statements are Profit and Loss, Balance Sheet and Statement of Cash Flows.

Variations in commodity prices are amplified by the business fixed cost and may severely affect margins if prices move unfavourably.

The Balance Sheet is a financial statement that summarizes a company's assets, liabilities and equity at a specific point in time.

The following formula set the balance between these three elements:

Assets = Liabilities + Shareholders' Equity

2110.body:
Theoretically, the price of a commodity is determined by the equilibrium of supply and demand. Realistically, it is quite costly for the stakeholders of a commodity market to constantly measure the equilibrium point in order to determine a fair price to pay or receive. As a result, there is no universal approach, and the price discovery mechanism used for each commodity is particular to each market and is usually the result of years of negotiations between the parties involved in the trade.

Notwithstanding the diversity, there are two main general trends that market participants adopt when determining prices for commodities: organised markets (like Futures markets) or price polls (price indices). When both using financial markets or price indices, market participants look for standardisation and transparency. Both the success of an index as standard price for a commodity and the development of derivatives markets depends on the final industry acceptance as a reliable source of pricing for their products.

The next chapter analyses organised markets.

In general, the final result of entering derivatives contracts is the generation of a new cash flow that will offset the cash flow at risk from the physical transaction. Therefore, once a physical transaction is hedged, the performance of the hedge i.e. the resulting cash flow must imperatively be viewed as a whole, whereby:

Cash flow of the hedged physical transaction = financial cash flow + physical cash flow

The hedge may also add risk if its not properly executed.

3150.body:
As Swaps may have multiple settlements, cash flows may also be multiple. The calculations to determine Cash Flows for Swaps are similar to the calculations for Futures Cash Flows.

When trading Exchange traded Swaps, Initial and Variation Margins will apply. OTC Swaps are usually traded under a Credit Line granted by the hedge provider and an ISDA contract which provides a Credit Support Annex (CSA) that establishes credit controls. The values of the cash flows for Initial and Variation Margins for Swaps are calculated using the following formulas:

Initial Margin for Swaps = Unitary Initial Margin * Quantity

Variation Margin for Swaps = MtM * Quantity

Initial Margins are deposited at the inception of each Swaps trade while Variation Margins are posted when the daily mark to market requires it.

In the case of a Futures contract, only the differences between the daily prices and the contract price are financially settled with the provider of the hedge. Usually, this cash flow is managed by the financial department of the company as it requires specific accounting treatment and specific regulated relationships with financial institutions. Some Exchanges and Clearing Houses always financially settle the contract at maturity, even if the contract was closed prior to that date.

Cash Flow from PnL = mark to market at maturity

Swaps: mark to market

The MtM is a measure of the fair market value of a financial Futures position.

MtM = (Value Swap(t) – Value Swap(0)) * exp (-r*T)

When the Swap is valued within its averaging period, the actual prices registered must be used to compute the current value of the Swap.

Swaps contracts have no associated direct costs and only pay Commissions to the broker on Exchange traded contracts. Opportunity costs, the bid-offer spread and the shape of the curve can be seen as indirect costs but they are not recognised in any cash flow.

Opportunity Costs

As with Futures, the main cost associated to the trading of Swaps is the opportunity cost. When entering a Swaps contract to hedge a physical position, the hedger gives up upside potential. This economic cost has no impact in the cash account.

Transaction Costs

Hedgers entering into Exchange traded Swaps contracts usually pay a commission charge that is negotiated with the Broker or established by the Exchange or Clearing House. Commissions may include Clearing House fees.
3150.title: Cash flows from the trade of Swaps

2270.body:
The widespread accepted model assumes that price changes are normally or log normally distributed. This is a clear and sometimes poor generalisation that may lead to dire results. The main problem regarding the use of the normal distribution is that it fails to capture extreme market movements that are less frequent but have potentially disastrous results. There are several ways to overcome this issue but it is first crucial to understand the distribution of returns for a particular commodity over a period of time.

VaR is one way of measuring Exposure.
2270.title: Note about probabilistic distributions

2720.body:
In order to close an open Futures position, an equal an opposite position must be bought/sold. If the position is not closed before the expiry or close date, the position is settled. Futures contracts, depending on their design as defined by the Exchange or market where they are traded, can be physically or cash settled.

Physical Settlement

A physically settled contract requires the parties to deliver or take delivery of the physical commodity at maturity. The long position will receive the material from the seller or the Exchange while the short position will deliver material to the buyer or to the Exchange. In the case of physically settled contracts, receiving or delivering products creates a natural link between paper (contracts) and physical (product). The idea behind this design is that this link guarantees convergence between both markets prices.

In cash settled contracts, only the net value of the cash flows is received or paid at maturity. For cash settlement, it is assumed that the index used to settle the contracts offers a representative and accepted reflection of the physical spot price.

Other settlement types:

- Exchange for Physical: An EFP is an agreement between parties holding opposite positions to enter into a bilateral agreement specifying the terms of a physical delivery. The parties need to notify the Clearing House or Exchange of their intentions.

- Alternative Delivery Procedure: An ADP is similar to an EFP but it is done subsequent of the termination of trading in the spot month contract. The parties need to notify the Clearing House or Exchange of their intentions.

3510.body:
The delta of an option is the sensitivity of the value of such option to changes in the price of the underlying commodity.

DELTA = Change value of the option / Change price underlying S

Delta is the first partial differential of the B-S formula with respect to the price of the underlying commodity (S).

DELTA Call option = N(d1)

DELTA Put option = N(d1) - 1

Value of Delta as a function of S (K=100)

Delta is an increasing function of the price of the underlying S. For any positive change in the priceS, the increase in the value of a Call will be strictly higher. The value of the Delta for a Call moves in the [0,1] range. Deltas below 0,5 corresponds to OTM options while Deltas above 0.5 corresponds to ATM options. For Puts, Deltas between -1 and -0.5 corresponds to ATM options while Deltas between -0.5 and -1 corresponds to OTM options.

The concept of Delta is not limited to options (non linear derivatives) and it can be used for Forwards, Futures and Physical positions. Deltas of such instruments can be summed up to obtain the Delta of the portfolio. Delta is not a measure of risk and it can give the same value to an extremely risky position and an extremely safe one (long call and short put with same Delta for example).
3510.title: Delta

3390.body:
Buying options contracts selectively changes a determined risk profile. The buyer of an option needs to pay a premium to acquire the right to exercise it only when the outcome is favourable. The seller will receive the incentive to concede such right.

On the expiry day, options have four basic profit and loss or payoff curves. Potential profits and losses for each option strategy depend on the price of the underlying forward contracts, strike prices, and the premium paid. In the case of a purchased option, the risk of loss is limited to the premium paid and the potential profit is unlimited. The contrary applies to written options; i.e. the risk of loss is unlimited while the potential profit is the premium received.

There are several formulaic developments to find the theoretical/hypothetical value of an option that are universally used in the financial and academic environments. The real value of the option is determined in the options market, where sellers and buyers interact exchanging risk profiles.

A future is an agreement to buy or sell a standardised grade and standardised quantity of a commodity to or from another party at a given price and a specified location at a future point in time. 2760.body:
The Spot is the price of a commodity for immediate delivery while the future is the price for future delivery. If carry costs for the commodity are known, there will be a precise relationship between spot and futures prices.

Fair Value, convergence and the no-arbitrage principle

The fair value for the Future price is the value of what it would cost to hold a physical asset until its delivery date. This is equal to the spot price plus costs of carry (storage costs, insurance, compounded interest rates, etc.) between the date of transaction and the maturity date.

Therefore, modeled in a simple way, forward prices are the result of the following equation:

F = S * exp((r – y) * T)

The Cost of Carry decreases as the future gets to its delivery date. As a result of the theoretical relationship explicated above, if interest rates are constant, Futures prices will converge to Spot prices and will be equal at maturity, when T=0.

In theory, if this relationship is violated during the life of the contract, there will be an arbitrage opportunity, resulting in riskless arbitrage profit.

Cash and carry arbitrage

If F > Spot * exp(r * T), then the Spot is relatively cheap so there will be an arbitrage opportunity in borrowing money and buying the commodity at spot prices, simultaneously selling the future contract. The commodity will be stored and delivered at maturity against the future contract. This action of bidding up the nearby while offering down the forward price would soon reduce the contango to a level that reflects the cost of funds to the most efficient investor in the market.

2360.body:
Understanding Basis Risk is fundamental to price risk management because basis risk results in potential over/under-performance of the hedge which leads to an economic and financial impact. Basis is the difference between the price of the underlying commodity which is being hedged and the price of the financial hedge.

Basis = Spot – Price of Financial Hedge

When hedging with Futures, Basis Risk appears when Spot and Futures Prices do not change by the same amount at the same time and possibly will not converge at maturity. In general terms, Basis Risk appears when the underlying commodity which is being hedged is not exactly represented by the underlying commodity of the derivative contract.

The basis can be dissected in its components and studied.
